documents.title: Academic Integrity - University Catalog
documents.summary: The catalog integrity policy names unsanctioned or undocumented AI help as cheating and plagiarism. AI is allowed only with instructor permission and full attribution. It also tells instructors to state in the syllabus when AI may be used.
documents.stance_why: AI is classed as cheating when 'unsanctioned and/or undocumented' and as plagiarism when used for central requirements 'without both the explicit permission of the instructor and complete attribution', so AI is banned unless the instructor permits it and it is cited.

units.why: The catalog lists 'work generated through unsanctioned and/or undocumented artificial intelligence (A.I.) assistance' as cheating, so it is a rule that binds students and a misconduct classification (P36, not P19, because it defines the violation rather than instructing how to work).
units.anchor: work generated through unsanctioned and/or undocumented artificial intelligence (A.I.) assistance.

units.why: Plagiarism is defined to include using 'A.I. text generators to perform central requirements of an assignment' without 'explicit permission of the instructor and complete attribution'; this is a misconduct definition (P36) that also sets a default of no AI unless permitted.
units.anchor: artificial intelligence (A.I.) text generators to perform central requirements of an assignment
units.policy: Plagiarism includes using A.I. text generators to perform central requirements of an assignment (reading, synthesizing, interpreting, writing, coding, programming) without both the explicit permission of the instructor and complete attribution and citation of A.I. assisted components.

units.why: The same definition makes AI use acceptable only with 'explicit permission of the instructor', which sets the fallback that AI is not allowed unless the instructor permits it (P06; P36 was considered but this unit is about the default when permission is absent).
units.anchor: without both the explicit permission of the instructor and complete attribution and citation
units.policy: Using A.I. text generators for central requirements of an assignment requires the explicit permission of the instructor.

units.why: The definition requires 'complete attribution and citation of A.I. assisted components', a disclosure duty on students (P24; P25 does not fit since no tool or prompt details are listed).
units.anchor: complete attribution and citation of A.I. assisted components
units.policy: Students must give complete attribution and citation of A.I. assisted components.

units.why: The grad section says 'It is the student's responsibility to discuss tools and resources with course instructors' before use unless authorized, i.e. ask before using (P10).
units.anchor: to discuss tools and resources with course instructors, advisors, and departments before use
units.policy: Graduate students discuss tools and resources with course instructors, advisors, and departments before use unless explicitly authorized in advance.

units.why: The same grad sentence says students must 'appropriately cite all resources and tools used in all academic work', a general disclosure duty covering AI tools (P24).
units.anchor: appropriately cite all resources and tools used in all academic work

units.why: The grad section states 'Acceptable academic resources vary across fields and departments', leaving resource permissions to fields and departments (P04).
units.anchor: Acceptable academic resources vary across fields and departments.

units.why: The faculty-roles list says the syllabus 'should also mention course policy regarding ... when, if ever, can artificial intelligence tools be used', so instructors are told to put an AI statement in the syllabus (P09).
units.anchor: when, if ever, can artificial intelligence tools be used
units.policy: The syllabus should mention course policy regarding when, if ever, artificial intelligence tools can be used.

units.why: 'The faculty member is encouraged to discuss the matter with the student' sets a talk-first step before escalating a violation; AI misuse is a listed violation so it applies (P57).
units.anchor: the faculty member is encouraged to discuss the matter with the student.

units.why: 'The student will be given an opportunity to respond to the allegation in writing (within 5 business days)' is a right to respond (P64) and covers AI-related allegations since AI use is a violation.
units.anchor: The student will be given an opportunity to respond to the allegation in writing

units.why: The consequences passage lists penalties from a warning up to 'university probation, suspension, or expulsion' for violations, which include unsanctioned AI use; this is a stated range of penalties (P37).
units.anchor: The most severe penalties may include university probation, suspension, or expulsion
units.frag_end: reportable to graduate/professional schools and outside agencies.

documents.unit: Center for Digital Innovation in Learning (CDIL)
documents.title: Teaching in an AI World
documents.summary: Faculty guidance from CDIL that recommends assessment redesign and open communication over detection software. It advises against AI detectors on accuracy, equity and FERPA grounds and leaves the permitted level of AI use to each instructor.
documents.stance_why: The page says it is 'not intended to serve as an official BC policy' and sets no rule on student AI use; it recommends faculty communicate their own position and redesign assessments, leaving the decision to instructors.

units.why: The page says it is 'not intended to serve as an official BC policy but rather as a clear outline of how CDIL recommends faculty answer this question', so it frames AI decisions as faculty-level recommendations (P04).
units.anchor: not intended to serve as an official BC policy
units.frag_start: This page provides BC faculty with

units.why: CDIL 'recommends a two-fold approach' beginning with 'Purposeful assignment and assessment design', a recommendation to redesign assessments around AI (P35).
units.anchor: Purposeful assignment and assessment design

units.why: The second part of the approach is 'Clear communication with students on the role of AI in your course and a clear explanation for why', i.e. telling students expectations and reasons (P09 closest: communicate AI expectations).
units.anchor: Clear communication with students on the role of AI in your course
units.frag_end: why you have taken this position.

units.why: The page says AI detection 'is not a viable solution' because 'it is impossible to prove whether or not work has been generated by AI', so detectors should not be relied on (P39).
units.anchor: it is impossible to prove whether or not work has been generated by AI
units.frag_start: Given the nature of Generative AI

units.why: It adds that vendors 'acknowledge the high rate of false positives in their detection of AI use', an accuracy reason against detectors (P39).
units.anchor: high rate of false positives in their detection of AI use in student work

units.why: Grammarly and text-to-voice 'are generally acceptable, increase educational accessibility', so AI-based writing aids are allowed; this is about prose tools, so P18 rather than P51.
units.anchor: These tools are generally acceptable, increase educational accessibility
units.policy: Widely used tools such as Grammarly or text-to-voice, which have used AI technology for years, are generally acceptable, increase educational accessibility and are crucial for many marginalized student groups' participation in education.

units.why: Running student work through detection software 'potentially puts their content into the public domain' and raises FERPA and IP concerns, a data-protection rule (P50; P39 considered, but the point here is student data).
units.anchor: Running student work through AI detection software potentially puts their content into the public domain

units.why: 'Boston College generally does not endorse the use of plagiarism detection software' is an institutional stance against detectors (P39).
units.anchor: Boston College generally does not endorse the use of plagiarism detection software
units.frag_start: As a result, Boston College generally
units.frag_end: faculty and students as it relates to academic integrity.

units.why: 'BC service units will be unable to provide technical assistance or guidance to faculty who independently opt to use plagiarism detection software' states a support limit tied to detectors (P39, closest type).
units.anchor: BC service units will be unable to provide technical assistance or guidance

units.why: The page notes the academic integrity policy 'has been updated (May 2024) to include specific language around the use of AI', a fact about the institutional rule (P36, because it ties AI to the integrity policy).
units.anchor: updated (May 2024) to include specific language around the use of AI

units.why: Step 1 says 'Explore AI for yourself' and understand how it works in your discipline, advice for instructors to learn AI before setting policy (P63).
units.anchor: Your first goal should be to understand the basics of how it works

units.why: For history, the page says AI 'output can be factually incorrect and amplify problematic historical accounts', a warning about AI errors and bias (P31).
units.anchor: the output can be factually incorrect and amplify problematic historical accounts

units.why: 'Communicate your expectations in a written statement in your course syllabus' directs instructors to put AI expectations in the syllabus (P09).
units.anchor: Communicate your expectations in a written statement in your course syllabus
units.policy: Instructors communicate their AI expectations in a written statement in the course syllabus and in person as a facilitated in-class discussion.

units.why: The page says the most important thing is 'an ongoing dialogue with your students about GenAI' including an in-class discussion; this is a communication practice not covered by P09 (syllabus statement), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: establish and maintain an ongoing dialogue with your students about GenAI
units.uncovered_note: Instructors hold an ongoing dialogue and in-class discussion with students about generative AI, beyond a written syllabus statement

units.why: Faculty believed syllabus statements banned AI but 'students' conceptions about what constitutes an AI tool did not match', an observation about how written statements fail (P55, evidence on practice).
units.anchor: students' conceptions about what constitutes an AI tool did not match those of faculty members
units.frag_start: We have encountered many faculty members

units.why: CDIL 'has developed a system of visual communication for clearly explaining expectations around student use of AI for different assignments', a named scheme of categories per assignment (P05).
units.anchor: a system of visual communication
units.policy: CDIL has developed a system of visual communication for clearly explaining expectations around student use of AI for different assignments.

units.why: 'Some learning outcomes might be AI-agnostic, so you might allow students to use AI freely' lets instructors decide per learning outcome, including free use (P04 chosen over P02 since it is conditional on outcome).
units.anchor: you might allow students to use AI freely
units.frag_start: Some learning outcomes might be AI-agnostic
units.frag_end: allow students to use AI freely.

units.why: Instructors are told to review learning outcomes and decide whether to change them or keep them 'because students need to be able to do them as they are fundamental', an assessment-design decision (P35).
units.anchor: Do you change the learning outcomes and devise new ones focused on what AI can
units.frag_start: Here you have a decision to make
units.frag_end: regardless of whether AI can do it or not?

units.why: 'Design outcomes that require students to meet benchmarks that AI cannot accomplish' advises redesigning assessment around AI (P35).
units.anchor: Design outcomes that require students to meet benchmarks that AI cannot accomplish.
units.frag_end: highly contemporary scenarios, working in teams, building social-emotional connections, or navigating scenarios with great ambiguity and complexity.

units.why: This approach 'removes you from evaluating whether students used AI' and focuses on whether expectations were met, i.e. not policing AI (P60).
units.anchor: removes you from evaluating whether students used AI in their work

units.why: 'Faculty need to rethink their assessments away from traditional formats' is an instruction to redesign assessments because of GenAI (P35).
units.anchor: faculty need to rethink their assessments away from traditional formats
units.frag_start: The availability of GenAI technology means

units.why: The page recommends 'process-based and project-based approaches' where multiple checkpoints with feedback are used, a redesign of grading around process (P35).
units.anchor: there should be multiple checkpoints for the paper with corresponding feedback sessions

units.why: It says GenAI 'cannot demonstrate the long-term reflection and articulation of cognitive development required in process- and project-based approaches', giving the rationale for process-based assessment (P35).
units.anchor: it cannot demonstrate the long-term reflection and articulation of cognitive development
units.frag_start: While GenAI is adept at producing text

units.why: Regular scaffolded activities and explaining 'how this work will help them be successful' make students 'less likely to feel tempted to turn to GenAI', a design and rationale practice (P41 considered; P35 chosen because the action is assignment redesign).
units.anchor: they are less likely to feel tempted to turn to GenAI
units.frag_start: However, if students clearly understand why

notes: Coder B. Generic integrity-process units (P57, P64, P37) are included because the catalog lists unsanctioned AI use as a violation; they are not AI-specific wording. Repeated grad/undergrad text and navigation skipped. No school or computing layer found; course layer deferred.
